        "text": "The elements of a vector space are called vectors, and we will sometimes use the column matrix notation\n\n$$\n\\left[\\begin{array}{c}\nz_{1}  \\tag{2.1}\\\\\n\\vdots \\\\\nz_{n}\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nto indicate a vector."

        "text": "Quantum mechanics is our main motivation for studying linear algebra, so we will use the standard notation of quantum mechanics for these concepts in the study of quantum mechanics.\nThe standard quantum mechanical notation for a vector in a vector space is the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n|\\psi\\rangle .\n\\tag{2.4}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\n$\\psi$ is a label for the vector (any label is valid, although we prefer to use simple labels like $\\psi$ and $\\varphi$ ).\nThe $|\\cdot\\rangle$ notation is used to indicate that the object is a vector.\nThe entire object $|\\psi\\rangle$ is sometimes called a ket, although we won't use that terminology often."

        "text": "A vector space also contains a special zero vector, which we denote by 0 .\nIt satisfies the property that for any other vector $|v\\rangle,|v\\rangle+0=|v\\rangle$.\nNote that we do not use the ket notation for the zero vector - it is the only exception we shall make.\nThe reason for making the exception is because it is conventional to use the 'obvious' notation for the zero vector, $|0\\rangle$, to mean something else entirely.\nThe scalar multiplication operation is such that $z 0=0$ for any complex number $z$."

        "text": "A vector subspace of a vector space $V$ is a subset $W$ of $V$ such that $W$ is also a vector space, that is, $W$ must be closed under scalar multiplication and addition."

        "start": 130,
        "end": 131,
        "text": "A spanning set for a vector space is a set of vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{n}\\right\\rangle$ such that any vector $|v\\rangle$ in the vector space can be written as a linear combination $|v\\rangle=\\sum_{i} a_{i}\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle$ of vectors\nin that set."

        "text": "For example, a spanning set for the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ is the set\n\n$$\n\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n1  \\tag{2.5}\\\\\n\\vdots \\\\\n0\n\\end{array}\\right] ; \\quad\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n0 \\\\\n1\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nsince any vector\n\n$$\n|v\\rangle=\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\na_{1}  \\tag{2.6}\\\\\na_{2}\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nin $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ can be written as a linear combination $|v\\rangle=a_{1}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+a_{2}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$ of the vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$.\nWe say that the vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$ span the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$.\n\nGenerally, a vector space may have many different spanning sets.\nA second spanning set for the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ is the set\n\n$$\n\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n1  \\tag{2.7}\\\\\n1\n\\end{array}\\right] ; \\quad\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left[\\begin{array}{r}\n1 \\\\\n-1\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nsince an arbitrary vector $|v\\rangle=\\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\\right)$ can be written as a linear combination of $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$,\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n|v\\rangle=\\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+\\frac{a_{1}-a_{2}}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle .\n\\tag{2.8}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$"

        "text": "A set of non-zero vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{n}\\right\\rangle$ are linearly dependent if there exists a set of complex numbers $a_{1}, \\ldots, a_{n}$ with $a_{i} \\neq 0$ for at least one value of $i$, such that\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\na_{1}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+a_{2}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle+\\cdots+a_{n}\\left|v_{n}\\right\\rangle=0 \\tag{2.9}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nA set of vectors is linearly independent if it is not linearly dependent.\nIt can be shown that any two sets of linearly independent vectors which span a vector space $V$ contain the same number of elements.\nWe call such a set a basis for $V$.\nFurthermore, such a basis set always exists.\nThe number of elements in the basis is defined to be the dimension of $V$.\nIn this book we will only be interested in finite dimensional vector spaces."

        "text": "A linear operator between vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is defined to be any function $A$ : $V \\rightarrow W$ which is linear in its inputs,\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\nA\\left(\\sum_{i} a_{i}\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right)=\\sum_{i} a_{i} A\\left(\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right) .\n\\tag{2.10}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nUsually we just write $A|v\\rangle$ to denote $A(|v\\rangle)$.\nWhen we say that a linear operator $A$ is defined on a vector space, $V$, we mean that $A$ is a linear operator from $V$ to $V$.\nAn important linear operator on any vector space $V$ is the identity operator, $I_{V}$, defined by the equation $I_{V}|v\\rangle \\equiv|v\\rangle$ for all vectors $|v\\rangle$.\nWhere no chance of confusion arises we drop the subscript $V$ and just write $I$ to denote the identity operator.\nAnother important linear operator is the zero operator, which we denote 0 .\nThe zero operator maps all vectors to\nthe zero vector, $0|v\\rangle \\equiv 0$."
